en: Padminī Ratnarakṣita Chapter 28: The Chapter on the Ritual of Homa (Homavidhi-paṭala) Nagoya Takaoka CA17 42r2–42r8 [The ritual procedure for the fire sacrifice is as follows: Having first prepared the sacrificial ground according to the prescribed rules, one should then construct the hearth (*kuṇḍa*). It should be circular, square, or triangular in shape, measuring one cubit, two cubits, or three cubits in size. One should then draw the lotus design (*padmacakra*) within it, using five-colored powders. Next, one should prepare the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and the pouring spoon (*sruva*), both made of *vikaṅkata* wood, with their handles fashioned from *śamī* wood. Having purified these implements with water, one should place them upon the hearth. Then, having kindled the fire with *samidh* fuel sticks of *udumbara*, *palāśa*, or *bilva* wood, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) while reciting the appropriate mantras. One should offer the oblations in the following sequence: first, the *āghāra* libations; then the *ājyabhāga* portions; followed by the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; and finally, the principal oblations (*homa*) dedicated to the specific deity. During this time, one should maintain a state of mental concentration (*samādhi*) and visualize the deity in the center of the fire. Having completed the offerings, one should perform the concluding rites (*pūrṇāhuti*), scattering flowers and incense before the fire. Then, having circumambulated the hearth three times while reciting auspicious verses, one should dismiss the deity. This concludes the chapter on the ritual of homa. *Padminī Ratnarakṣita* *Homavidhi-paṭala*, Chapter 28. Nagoya Takaoka CA17 42r2–42r8.

Regarding the questions and answers concerning restraint (*nigraha*) and favor (*anugraha*), he says "Now," and so forth. "The mantra" refers to the heart-mantra of the Blessed One. "In the fire of Caṇḍālī" means in the fire brought from the house of a Caṇḍāla. "At the great night" means at midnight. "In the fire of the Piśācas" means in the fire of the cremation ground. "Dwelling in the upper direction of the northwest" means mounted upon the mandala of Vāyu.

In order to provide an answer to the request for subduing and conversion, he said, beginning with "Then," and so forth. "Mantra" refers to the heart-mantra of the Blessed One. "In the fire of the outcaste" means in a fire taken from the house of an outcaste. "At midnight" means at the time of midnight. "The fire of the flesh-eaters" means the fire of a charnel ground. "Abiding in the direction above the wind."
This means that he is mounted upon the mandala of wind.

This is what is meant: one who desires to perform an attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) should face the northwest, offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*), and assume the yoga of the Red Saṃvara. Seated in the *lalitāsana* posture, he should visualize the object of the rite (*sādhya*) mounted upon a wind-mandala. With Khaṇḍarohā—emerging from the seed-syllable in his heart and holding a hook and a noose—he binds the [object's] throat with the noose and pierces the heart with the hook. Visualizing the [object] being drawn forth, he should interpose the mantra "Jaḥ! Attract so-and-so! Jaḥ! and, while reciting the heart-mantra or any other desired mantra, [he should write] on birch bark with his own ring finger, using blood and *gorocanā*.

Having drawn the form of the person to be accomplished with a stylus made of *dhuttūra* wood, having placed it upon a beautiful, single-piece, unblemished skull-cup, and having covered it with a cloth, one should offer oblations of red *karavīra* flowers over it, each preceded by the recitation of the mantra; thus, one effects attraction.

It is taught as follows: One who desires to summon [the deity] should visualize [himself] as wind, offer the *bali* oblation, and, possessing the yoga of Red Cakrasaṃvara, remain in a playful posture. Then, the one to be accomplished—mounted upon a wind mandala—is bound at the neck with the noose from the hand of Khaṇḍarohā, who has emerged from the seed-syllable at [one's own] heart and holds a hook and a noose.

One should visualize [the deity] drawing [the target] in by piercing the heart with an iron hook, and recite the desired mantra—such as the expanded essence mantra "DZA: [Name] ĀKARṢAYA DZA:"—as appropriate.

On a *gro ga* leaf, having clearly drawn the image of the subject with one’s own blood and *gi wang*, using a pen made from the wood of the *thang phrom* tree, place it in a beautiful, single-piece skull-cup free of cracks; cover it with cloth, and if one performs a fire offering (*homa*) upon it with red *karavīra* flowers while preceded by the recitation of the mantra for each individual offering, [the subject] will be summoned.

Now, another method of attraction is also easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "having drawn the *bhaga*": the word "in front" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding "with the left hand": it should be understood as "pressing down. Regarding "on the upward-moving wind": this refers to a whirlwind. Regarding "the garment of a *preta*": this is the shroud of a corpse. Regarding "*nāgamallikā*": this is a lamp made from *nāgakesara* wood in the shape of a jasmine flower; some say it is a lamp made of lead. Regarding "*hastilaḍḍa*": this is elephant dung.

Furthermore, there is another application for summoning, which is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "having clearly drawn the bhaga," the word "in front" is the ellipsis. Regarding "with the left hand," it should be understood as "having pressed down. "An upward-rising whirlwind" refers to the wind mandala. "The garment of a preta" refers to the garment of a corpse.
The "nāga lamp" refers to a lamp made from the wood of the *nāgakeśara* tree; some say it refers to a "jātī lamp. "Elephant dung" refers to that which is associated with elephants.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-eighth chapter. [curl] ||
This is the explanation of the twenty-eighth chapter.
